rationale: The historical account reports acute urge sensations without a controlled comparison. One common-sage extract trial reports an inconclusive urogenital composite and another an inconclusive urinary leakage item (p=.369). Neither discusses separate urgency frequency. Two different-species root extracts have inconclusive week-12 urgency items. Traditional common-sage renal use includes diuretic purposes, without measured symptom change.

The craniotomy supplement gives inconclusive patient anxiety VAS comparisons for ginger extract. A healthy-adult root powder comparison is inconclusive, and the SSRI adjunct abstract conflicts with itself about direction. The Ginger-PD registry has no standalone anxious-mood result. Simon's artificial permeability study and the newer injected 6-gingerol concentration study concern constituent passage or exposure. They do not measure anxiety. A firsthand report describes calming after grated ginger with uncertain preparation, timing and diagnosis. Rodent extract behavior supplies indirect evidence. The available comparisons leave the effect of grated ginger on diagnosed Parkinson anxiety open. The newer Jambi review attributes ginger to traditional blood-pressure use rather than anxiety and supplies no clinical Parkinson result. In the chemotherapy trial, all three HADS anxiety intervals cross zero. The separate migraine extract trial observed similar day-90 Beck means. These are original randomized comparisons of different preparations in other populations.
